cards.say: The more an agent can do on its own, the more it can get wrong on its own. **Guardrails** are the rules that keep its actions inside a safe range.

cards.q: Match each guardrail to what it limits
pairs: Which tools or data the agent can touch
A person signs off before a risky action runs
How many actions it can take per minute
A record of every action, for review later
cards.why: Each guardrail limits a different kind of risk: reach, timing, speed, and accountability after the fact.

cards.q: An agent can send emails for you. What's the safest default?
options: Have it draft the email and wait for your approval
Never let it touch email at all
cards.why: Drafting and waiting keeps the speed benefit while a person still catches mistakes before anything goes out. Blocking it entirely gives up the upside for no reason.

cards.q: Myth or fact: giving an agent broader permissions always makes it more useful.
cards.why: Broader permissions raise capability and risk together. Scoping access to just what the task needs is usually the better trade.

cards.q: One of these habits is actually risky. Tap it.
sentences: Start a new agent with the narrowest access it needs.
Give a brand-new agent full access on day one so nothing gets blocked.
Log every action so mistakes can be traced later.
cards.why: Starting broad means a bug or a bad prompt can do maximum damage on day one. Start narrow, and widen access deliberately once it's earned trust.

cards.q: Put a safe rollout of a new agent capability in order
steps: Test the action in a sandbox with fake data
Add it live, but with a required human approval step
Watch real runs closely for a while
Remove the approval step once it's proven reliable
cards.why: Sandbox, then human-checked, then supervised, then autonomous. Trust is earned in stages, not assumed on day one.
